Traditional institutional voting systems are frequently plagued by challenges ranging from high administrative costs and logistical bottlenecks to critical concerns regarding security, transparency, and the integrity of results. This project presents the development of an "Online Voting System with Enhanced Security and Transparency," a web-based artifact designed to address these vulnerabilities through a robust digital framework.

Utilizing the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology and an Iterative Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) model, the system was built using a decoupled 3-tier architecture consisting of a React.js frontend, a Node.js backend, and a MySQL relational database. To ensure maximum data integrity and voter privacy, the project implements 3rd Normal Form (3NF) database normalization and a structural isolation strategy that prevents direct links between voter identities and cast ballots.

The system’s core security is bolstered by an "Electoral Roll" (Voter Registry) logic, which limits participation to authorized student IDs for specific elections. Furthermore, transparency is achieved through the integration of verifiable Audit Logs and real-time turnout analytics, allowing administrators to monitor election health without compromising the anonymity of the vote. Advanced protections, such as

password hashing, JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for role-based access control, and time-bucketing of ballot timestamps to prevent side-channel correlation, were implemented to defend against common cyber threats.

The result is a scalable, user-friendly, and highly secure platform that promotes democratic participation while providing a verifiable audit trail. This research demonstrates that through the strategic application of modern web technologies and rigorous architectural design, institutional elections can achieve a high standard of transparency and reliability in a digital-first environment.

Elections remain one of the most important pillars of democratic governance, allowing citizens or organizational members to express their preferences through the selection of representatives or policy choices. Traditional paper-based voting systems have served this purpose for decades, but they are prone to human error, logistical inefficiency, and manipulation

As societies and institutions increasingly depend on digital infrastructure, there has been a growing demand for electronic or online voting systems that improve accuracy, efficiency, and transparency in elections (Shahzad et al., 2020).

An online voting system (also referred to as e-voting) allows eligible voters to cast ballots securely through the internet using digital authentication and encryption technologies. These systems aim to simplify election administration, reduce costs, and promote accessibility
especially for individuals unable to reach physical polling stations.

However, e-voting introduces new challenges. Concerns such as identity verification, data privacy, vote tampering, and network security must be carefully addressed to ensure that digital elections maintain or exceed the integrity of traditional voting methods (Ali & Al-Harby, 2021). Recent advances in encryption, blockchain technology, and secure web frameworks have shown promise in achieving end-to-end verifiability while preserving voter anonymity (Heiberg et al., 2020).

Therefore, this study proposes the design and implementation of an Online Voting System with Enhanced Security and Transparency, leveraging modern web technologies to demonstrate how secure, auditable, and user-friendly digital voting can be achieved at an institutional level.
Despite the technological progress in digital communication, many elections

continue to rely on manual voting systems that are slow, costly, and susceptible to fraud. Studies have shown that even some electronic systems implemented worldwide have faced vulnerabilities ranging from weak authentication to server compromise and lack of verifiability

For small- and medium-scale elections, such as university student government or corporate board elections, available solutions are often inadequate, lacking strong security mechanisms and transparent result auditing. This creates a need for an online voting platform that can combine security, integrity, and transparency while maintaining usability for ordinary voters

This research uses theories from information security and electronic governance to support the design of a secure and transparent voting platform.

Online voting relies on mathematical assurance and not on institutional trust. PKI represents the foundation of authentication and integrity of data, based on the work of Rivest & Wack (2006). Every voter will have a private-public key pair, which allows secure vote transmission and verification, but not identification.

According to Bovens, 2007, transparency makes processes more visible to stakeholders, hence enhancing accountability. In e-voting, this theory supports the openness in the audit mechanisms that would permit voters, observers, and administrators to verify system behaviour while maintaining privacy.
Taken together, these theories can form a basis for a socio-technical, cryptographically sound, and transparent e-voting architecture suitable for use within institutions and organizations.
2.3 Review of Related Literature and Empirical Studies

Research on e-voting systems encompasses such issues as technical security and user trust, through to real-world implementations. The following review synthesizes the key empirical and related studies, organized by their primary thematic focus.

The cryptographic underpinning of e-voting is where a large body of the literature rests. Rivest & Wack (2006) provided a basic building block, "software independence," meaning a system’s correctness should not depend on any single software component, a central tenet for modern designs. Following this, Zissis & Lekkas (2012) proposed a secure framework for e-voting based on a layered cloud architecture using cryptographic primitives for end-to-end integrity and voter anonymity. More recently, Cortier & Kremer (2018) have been working on formal verification of such cryptographic protocols, showing that model-checking tools are able to find design-level vulnerabilities before deployment.

The arrival of blockchain has set off serious research into decentralized e-voting. Heiberg, Laud, & Vinkel (2020) proposed a verifiable Internet voting system using blockchain-style append-only logs, showing that cryptographic proofs can ensure voter privacy while enabling public verification. Shahzad, Kang, & Lee (2020) introduced a blockchain-based architecture using Ethereum smart contracts that securely record and validate ballots.
Comparative analyses, like that of Jameel et al. (2022), conclude that decentralized applications outperform centralized databases on auditability and tamper resistance issues. Others have focused
on optimization: Chakraborty et al. (2019) designed a lightweight blockchain framework suitable for institutional elections. However,
(2018) pointed out that though blockchain strengthens auditability, there are challenges to its scalability and verification of voter identity.
According to Socio-Technical Systems Theory, researchers emphasize that usability and trust are as imperative as technical security.

& Stark (2015) did a study in Germany focused on how usability and trust are essential in the successful adoption of technology. Acemyan et al. (2018) undertook usability testing of end-to-end verifiable systems, Helios, and STAR-Vote, and discovered that clearer interfaces and feedback mechanisms greatly enhanced voter confidence and error detection.

This adoption challenge is also influenced by regional factors: In studying e-voting adoptions in Asian countries, Zhao & Chan (2020) found that infrastructure readiness, regulatory support, and cultural trust strongly influence the success of implementation.

(2021) further investigated how developing economies might leverage cloud and mobile infrastructures in attempting to deliver secure digital elections, bringing into focus related questions about governance frameworks.
Analysis of real-world systems provides invaluable insight. Alvarez, Hall, &

(2013) examined international Internet voting projects and determined that while the systems increase ease of access for overseas voters, the central problems pertain to the secrecy of ballots and dependable authentication. Of particular note was the extensive security analysis of Estonia's

country-wide Internet voting system provided by Springall et al. (2014), showing client-side vulnerabilities and a lack of verification mechanisms that made manipulation of votes possible. The results of such findings have led many scholars to recommend hybrid approaches. A large-scale review by Ali and Al-Harby (2021) of the contemporary e-voting technologies concluded that hybrid systems, merging traditional cryptography with blockchain, often provide much stronger resistance to insider attacks and better scalability than the purely centralized approach.

A review of the related literature indicated that online voting systems have evolved from simple web-based ballot systems to sophisticated, cryptographically secured, and sometimes blockchain-enabled architectures. On a conceptual level, most of the reviewed works agree that e-voting can increase accessibility, efficiency, and transparency if well implemented. The theoretical models, such as the end-to-end verifiability framework and software independence principle, have provided the basis necessary for secure and auditable systems.

Despite these advances, a gap in the literature is clear: though decentralized blockchain systems are highly transparent Heiberg et al. (2020), Shahzad et al. (2020), and though formal cryptographic models are secure Rivest & Wack (2006), Zissis & Lekkas (2012), there remains a pent-up need for systems that are highly usable Acemyan et al. (2018), scalable, and resistant to client-side vulnerabilities Springall et al. (2014). Many scholars point to hybrid systems as the most promising path forward Ali & Al-Harby (2021).
These findings constitute direct justification for the proposed system in this work. An Online Voting System based on a modern, robust client-server architecture (React.js and Node.js) will try

to fill the security and usability gaps on the client side. In addition, with a secure relational database, MySQL, and strong encryption, this solution is practical, centralized but verifiable, and strikes a good balance among security, transparency, and accessibility for institutional use in accord with global best practices.

For proper management of the software development process, this project uses the Iterative Software Development Life Cycle model.

The Iterative model is one in which the system is developed in cycles. Every cycle can be built upon to add more functionality to finally develop the complete system. This model is preferred over the Waterfall model for the given project for the following reasons:
: Our first concern is security. The Iterative model makes it possible for us to develop and strengthen basic security components (e.g., user login and encryption of votes) in the first iteration.

: It tackles the largest risks earliest. By developing the voting and tallying mechanism core logic in the first cycle itself, we can establish the integrity of our system before adding other functionalities.
: Feedback can be incorporated at the end of each iteration with the flexibility to refine the interface (React
/Tailwind) and logic (Node.js) to ensure it is more accurate.
: A functional prototype of the system can be created quickly that is functional but with little detail.

This chapter presents a summary of the entire research work carried out in this project. The study focused on the design and implementation of an "Online Voting System with Enhanced Security and Transparency" aimed at solving the logistical bottlenecks and integrity concerns associated with traditional voting methods.

The research began in Chapter One with the identification of problems such as high administrative costs and lack of verifiable audit trails. Objectives were formulated to design a secure architecture that ensures voter anonymity and data integrity. Chapter Two reviewed relevant literature and conceptual frameworks, highlighting the importance of cryptographic hashing and decentralized logic in modern digital democracy.

In Chapter Three, the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology and an Iterative SDLC model were adopted. The technical design utilized a decoupled 3-tier architecture consisting of a React.js frontend, a Node.js backend, and a MySQL database. Key security features discussed included structural isolation between user identities and ballots, and the implementation of a Voter Registry to gate participation.

Chapter Four focused on the implementation and rigorous testing of the system. The results demonstrated that the developed system performs efficiently, handling authentication via JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and processing votes through atomic database transactions. The system was tested against various scenarios, including unauthorized access attempts and double-voting
simulations, ensuring that the final artifact is robust, reliable, and user-friendly.

This research work has demonstrated that the application of a 3-tier, computer-based architecture can significantly improve the efficiency, accuracy, and transparency of institutional elections. By separating the presentation, logic, and data layers, the system provides a reliable solution to the challenges of manual voting.
The project successfully met its core goals:
Enforced through a database design where no direct foreign key link exists between the Users and Votes tables.
Guaranteed through the use of an "Electoral Roll" (Voter Registry) and verifiable Audit Logs that track all administrative actions.
Achieved through an analytics dashboard that provides instant turnout statistics without compromising individual ballot secrecy.
In conclusion, the developed system proves to be a valuable contribution to the field of information technology, offering a scalable framework for conducting secure and transparent digital elections.
Based on the findings and the successful implementation of this research, the following recommendations are made:
The system should be deployed for real-life use in academic and corporate organizations to fully utilize its benefits in reducing electoral costs and
Stakeholders and voters should undergo brief training sessions to ensure they understand the digital interface and the security measures protecting their privacy.
Future administrators should conduct regular security audits of the system’s logs to maintain long-term institutional trust.
The system should be updated regularly to address emerging web vulnerabilities and to ensure compatibility with evolving browser technologies.
Further research can be carried out to integrate the system with existing institutional databases (e.g., Student Information Systems) to automate the voter registry process.
Future researchers are encouraged to build upon this work by exploring more advanced cryptographic technologies. Potential enhancements include:
Utilizing facial recognition or fingerprint scanning to replace password-based authentication for higher security.
Transitioning the MySQL "Ballot Box" to a distributed ledger to provide a decentralized, immutable record of every vote.
Incorporating machine learning algorithms to detect behavioural anomalies or bot-like voting patterns in real-time.
These advancements will help in making the system more robust, scalable, and suitable for wider, national-level applications.
